newsitem.title: USA: Philip Morris, RJR debt mixed on settlement news.
newsitem.headline: Philip Morris, RJR debt mixed on settlement news.

text.p: RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp and Philip Morris Cos Inc debt met Friday's landmark settlement between U.S. states and the tobacco industry with a mixed reaction, corporate bond traders said.
Players said initial reaction to the settlement was mixed with the intermediate coupons seen a touch tighter and longer paper a bit wider.
"The debt is slightly better...it has tightened throughout the day," said one high-grade trader of intermediate paper.
"Right now it's tough to gauge as it is a Friday afternoon and many players are gone."
RJR Nabisco 8-3/4 paper due 2005 tightened to a 184 basis points bid, 182 basis points offer. That compares with a 225 bid, 200 offer, a few days ago, traders said.

However, players said the size of the settlement will likely weigh on the company's financial profile and for that reason some were surprised RJR bonds rallied as strongly as they had in the past few days.
"We weren't anticipating this because the settlement's still going to be a financial strain no matter how you slice it or dice it for a BBB credit," another trader said.

Philip Morris' 7.20 percent debt due 2007 tightened another five basis points to a 75 bid, 72 offer. The paper has tightened a total of 10 basis points since Wednesday when news hit the market that a settlement was nearing, traders said.
Players said longer-dated paper was a touch wider. Philip Morris' 30-year paper, which was trading at a 101 bid before the settlement widened to a 105 bid, traders said.
"I think the settlement's a little harsher than people had anticipated," said a trader of longer-dated tobacco paper.
"As you see more details of the settlement emerge you'll see why bonds have widened out."
Analysts said it was difficult to accurately interpret investor reaction to the late-Friday announcement that the tobacco industry had agreed to pay states $368.5 billion over 25 years.

"You will be able to gauge the reaction better when people come in on Monday after digesting the information," said one tobacco industry debt analyst, who was struggling to fully assess the implications of the agreement.
Talks between tobacco industry representatives and the state attorneys general had been ongoing since early April.
Meanwhile, players will keep a watchful eye on the impact of the settlement on tobacco firms' credit ratings.
In April, credit rating agency Standard & Poor's placed the ratings of tobacco firms with U.S. litigation exposure under review for possible downgrade.
Of particular interest will be RJR Nabisco debt, which is currently rated only one notch above junk bond status at Baa3/BBB-minus, by Moody's Investors Service and S&P, respectively.
Philip Morris' senior unsecured debt is currently rated A2 by Moody's and single-A by S&P.
